blurb: Dr. K hosts a guided tour of the 10-K: the annual report every U.S. public company files, the four Items that matter most, and why these documents are so hard to read that we needed to build ADAM in the first place.
intro: Welcome aboard — I'm Dr. K, and before we argue about what a disclosure means, we need to know where disclosures live. This episode is a guided tour of the 10-K: the annual report every U.S. public company files, the four Items that matter most, and why these documents are so hard to read that we needed to build ADAM in the first place.

body: A Form 10-K is the annual report most U.S. public companies must file each year with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The company writes it, the SEC sets the topics and their fixed order, and anyone can read it for free on EDGAR, the SEC's public filing database.

It is not a marketing brochure. The chief executive and chief financial officer must certify its accuracy — and the filing has a deadline: 60 days after fiscal year-end for large accelerated filers (public float of $700 million or more), 75 days for accelerated filers, and 90 days for everyone else.

The 10-K is long because it has to be: it must cover the business, its risks, management's view of performance, and audited financial statements, all in one document. That length is exactly the problem ADAM was built to attack.
lessons.tip: If you ever open a real 10-K, start with the table of contents and jump straight to Item 1A and Item 7 — the two narrative sections ADAM reads. The rest is reference material until you need it.

body: Item 1 — Business: what the company does — its main products and services, subsidiaries, and markets, plus competition, regulation, labour, operating costs, and seasonality.

Item 1A — Risk Factors: the most significant risks to the company and its securities, generally listed in order of importance. It focuses on the risks themselves — not on how the company plans to address them. Risks can be economy-wide, industry-wide, or unique to the firm. (Illustrative paraphrase, not a company quote: “Our business faces risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations, including competition, supply disruption, regulation, and litigation.”)

Item 7 — MD&A (Management's Discussion and Analysis): management's own-words perspective on the past year — operations and results, liquidity and capital resources, known trends and uncertainties, material changes from prior periods, and critical accounting judgments. (Illustrative paraphrase: “Revenue rose this year because volumes increased, partly offset by higher costs; liquidity remains adequate, but a known trend in input prices could affect future margins.”)

Item 8 — Financial Statements: the audited numbers — income statement, balance sheets, statement of cash flows, and statement of stockholders' equity, plus explanatory notes, prepared under GAAP and audited by an independent accountant. ADAM reads Items 1A and 7 because they are the narrative-heavy sections — and because they have different linguistic baselines: risk-factor language sounds different from management's own story, and a fair reader has to know which room it is standing in.
lessons.tip: Item 1A warns you about what could go wrong. Item 7 tells you what did happen and what management thinks comes next. Confuse the two and you will read a warning as a confession.

body: Three things make 10-Ks hard. Volume: narrative sections are long, and reviewing them paragraph by paragraph is slow and costly. Repetition: material language is mixed with prior-year carryover, boilerplate, and legal caution. Interpretive difficulty: tone, economic direction, and informativeness are not the same construct — a paragraph can sound negative, describe no real economic harm, and carry no new information, all at once.

ADAM's empirical setting is deliberately broad: 55 firms, five from each of 11 GICS sectors, over 10 years (2016–2025) — 550 firm-year 10-Ks yielding 179,623 focal paragraphs: 94,031 from Item 1A and 85,592 from Item 7. Another 32,407 paragraphs from 2014–2015 filings serve only as historical context, so the system can tell what is new from what is carried over.

The unit of analysis is the contextualized paragraph object: every paragraph stays linked to its firm, year, section, sector, prior-year context, peer context, and provenance — so any conclusion can be traced back to the exact words it came from.

A note on the numbers: slide 10 of the ADAM deck also prints “143,372 focal paragraphs.” The Item counts on the same slide sum to 179,623 (94,031 + 85,592), which is the figure used throughout this site.

game.done: Four for four. You can tell a warning about the future from an explanation of the past — which is the first skill a disclosure reader needs.
game.hint: Not quite — ask: is this a risk that might happen, or management explaining what did happen?
game.intro: Four short passages, written in the style of a 10-K (illustrative paraphrases, not real company quotes). Sort each into the Item it belongs to — Item 1A (Risk Factors) or Item 7 (MD&A).

items.t: “Our business faces risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations, including competition, supply disruption, regulation, and litigation.”
items.why: It lists risks themselves — competition, supply, regulation, litigation — without explaining how the company will address them. That is Item 1A's job.

items.t: “Revenue rose this year because volumes increased, partly offset by higher costs; liquidity remains adequate, but a known trend in input prices could affect future margins.”
items.why: Management explaining results, liquidity, and a known trend in its own words — classic MD&A.

items.t: “Changes in tax law or trade rules in the countries where we operate could materially increase our costs or limit our ability to sell.”
items.why: A potential threat, stated as a risk — not a discussion of what actually happened this year.

items.t: “Management believes cash on hand plus operating cash flow will fund operations for the next twelve months, although planned capital spending is expected to rise.”
items.why: A forward look at liquidity and capital resources from management's perspective — MD&A territory.

game.title: Dr. K Challenge: Which Item is this passage from?

lessons.h: Why 10-Ks are hard — and the data ADAM reads
lessons.tip: Boilerplate is the enemy of attention: language repeated unchanged for years looks serious and means almost nothing new. ADAM's Context & Quality Agent exists to catch exactly that.

outro: You can now open a 10-K and know where you are — Business, Risk Factors, MD&A, Financial Statements — and why the same paragraph can look scary and say very little. Next, the dictionary that taught computers to read these filings — and the trap it walks into.

quiz.q: Which Item of a 10-K lists the company's most significant risks, generally in order of importance?
quiz.why: Item 1A — Risk Factors is the risk list, ordered by importance, and it describes the risks themselves rather than how the company addresses them. Item 1 covers the business, Item 7 is management's view of performance, and Item 8 holds the audited statements.

quiz.q: ADAM's focal data covers 55 firms over 2016–2025. How many firm-year 10-Ks and focal paragraphs is that?
quiz.why: 55 firms × 10 years = 550 firm-year 10-Ks, yielding 179,623 focal paragraphs (94,031 from Item 1A + 85,592 from Item 7 = 179,623). The 143,372 printed on slide 10 is a slide error — the item counts sum to 179,623 — and 32,407 is the separate 2014–2015 historical context.

opts: Because Item 1A is unaudited and cannot be trusted
Because tone, economic direction, and informativeness are different things — negative wording can be routine boilerplate
Because all Item 1A language is legally required to sound negative
Because Item 7 always reverses what Item 1A says
quiz.q: A paragraph in Item 1A sounds very negative. Why is that NOT, on its own, evidence of bad news for the company?
quiz.why: Tone, economic direction, and informativeness are three separate constructs. A negative-sounding paragraph can be routine risk-factor boilerplate — the same words as last year, no new information — which is why ADAM separates the three instead of collapsing them into one score.
